column1: # Every architecture this fork builds for, with the toolchain that builds it,
# the emulator that runs it, and the path each dispatcher must land on.
# The list is data so that adding an architecture is an edit here rather than to
# the workflow, and so that a developer and CI run the same check. bench/arch-
# check.sh reads a row; .github/workflows/ci.yml turns the file into its matrix.
# Columns, tab separated:
#   1 name        label for the row
#   2 toolchain   openwrt tarball URL, apt:<package>, or - for the host compiler
#   3 sha256      sha256 of that tarball, or - when there is none to pin
#   4 cpu_flags   appended to the compiler command, or -
#   5 qemu        emulator and CPU model, or - to run natively
#   6 addmul1     path the multiply must choose
#   7 xor_tile    path the cook XOR must choose
#   8 crc32c      path the checksum must choose
# "any" declines to hold a column. Only x86_64 uses it, because its dispatch
# follows whatever chip the runner has; the cpu-dispatch job pins that down
# against named CPU models instead. An empty column is a failure, not a skip.
# The two 32-bit ARM rows are a matched pair, and both carry no cpu_flags on
# purpose. OpenWrt defines no CPU_CFLAGS for arm and passes no -mfpu anywhere;
# it configures a per-target toolchain and lets the compiler default carry the
# FPU. Naming a flag here would test the flag rather than the toolchain the feed
# actually uses. The a15 row proves the vector paths are reached, the a9 row
# proves they stay out of a build for a core with no NEON unit.
# An unverified toolchain download builds the binaries we ship from whatever
# the network returned. Every tarball is pinned; the download step refuses on a
# mismatch rather than carrying on. Rows using an apt package or the host
# compiler have nothing to pin and record -.
# name
aarch64
mips
powerpc
armv7-neon
armv7-scalar
riscv64
